cards.note: Herod the tetrarch is reproved over Herodias, his brother's wife, and all his evils.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Herod adds this to all and shuts John up in prison.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: When all the people were baptized and Jesus too, while he prayed, heaven was opened.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: The Spirit descends in bodily form like a dove and the voice says 'You are my beloved Son' with God's pleasure in him.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Both give Jesus' age as about thirty and the line Joseph, Heli; the Latin card also includes Mathat, which the Greek card places in the next verse.
cards.cause: Verse division: the name Mathat falls at the end of this Latin verse and at the start of the next Greek verse.

cards.note: Levi, Melchi, Janne (Jannai) and Joseph agree; the Greek card also opens with Matthat, which the Latin card has in the previous verse.
cards.cause: Verse division: the name Mathat falls in the previous Latin verse and at the start of this Greek verse.

cards.note: Mathathias, Amos, Nahum, Hesli (Esli) and Nagge (Naggai) agree; the differences are spelling of names.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Mahath, Mathathias and Semei agree; Latin has 'Joseph' and 'Juda' where the Greek has Josech and Joda.
cards.cause: A different textual reading in the Latin tradition for two names; some Greek manuscripts also read Joseph and Juda.

cards.note: Joanna, Resa, Zorobabel, Salathiel and Neri match the Greek names; the differences are spelling.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Melchi, Addi, Cosan, Elmadan and Her match the Greek names apart from spelling.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Jesus, Eliezer, Jorim, Mathat and Levi agree on both sides.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Simeon, Juda, Joseph, Jona and Eliakim agree apart from the spelling of Jona (Jonam).
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Melea, Menna, Mathatha, Natham and David agree apart from spelling.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Jesse, Obed, Booz and Naasson agree; Latin has 'Salmon' where the Greek has Sala.
cards.cause: A different textual reading; the Latin agrees with Greek manuscripts that read Salmon.

cards.note: Latin lists Aminadab, Aram, Esron; the Greek has Amminadab, Admin, Arni, Hezron, adding a generation and differing in name.
cards.cause: A different textual reading; the Latin has the single name Aram, as many Greek manuscripts do, while the Greek text used here has Admin and Arni.

cards.note: Jacob, Isaac, Abraham, Thare (Terah) and Nachor (Nahor) agree; the differences are spelling of names.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Sarug, Ragau, Phaleg, Heber and Sale are the Greek Serug, Reu, Peleg, Eber and Shelah in Latin spelling.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Cainan, Arphaxad, Sem, Noah and Lamech agree on both sides.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Methusale, Henoch, Jared, Malaleel and Cainan match the Greek names apart from spelling.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Henos, Seth, Adam and God close the genealogy on both sides.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returns from the Jordan; Latin says he was led 'by the Spirit into the desert' (a Spiritu in desertum), the Greek in the Spirit in the wilderness.
cards.cause: A difference of construction; the Latin agrees with Greek manuscripts reading 'into the wilderness'.

cards.note: Forty days of temptation by the devil, eating nothing, and hunger at the end appear on both sides.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: The devil tells the Son of God to command this stone to become bread.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Latin adds 'but by every word of God' (sed in omni verbo Dei); the Greek quotes only that man shall not live by bread alone.
cards.cause: A different textual reading; the Latin has the longer quotation found in some Greek manuscripts, which the Greek text used here lacks.

cards.note: Latin says the devil led him 'into a high mountain' (in montem excelsum); the Greek says only that he took him up before showing the kingdoms.
cards.cause: A different textual reading; the Latin has the mountain, as some Greek manuscripts do, while the Greek text used here lacks it.

cards.note: The offer of authority and glory agrees; Latin uses the plural 'they are delivered' (tradita sunt) where the Greek says it has been handed over, and does not name the devil.
cards.cause: A difference of number and a pronoun for a name in the Latin rendering.

cards.note: If Jesus worships before the devil, all will be his, on both sides.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Jesus answers that it is written: worship the Lord your God and serve him alone.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: The devil sets Jesus on the temple pinnacle and tells the Son of God to throw himself down from here.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Both cite God's charge to his angels to guard him; Latin has the perfect 'mandavit' (has given charge) where the Greek has the future 'will command'.
cards.cause: A difference of tense in the Latin rendering of the quotation.

cards.note: The angels bear him up in their hands lest he strike his foot against a stone.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Jesus answers that it is said: you shall not tempt (test) the Lord your God.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Every temptation ended, the devil departs from him until a time; 'tempus' and the Greek 'opportune time' differ only in English wording.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Jesus returns to Galilee in the power of the Spirit and his fame spreads through the region.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: He teaches in their synagogues and is glorified by all; 'magnificabatur' differs only in English wording.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Jesus comes to Nazareth, enters the synagogue on the Sabbath as was his custom and stands up to read.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: The book of Isaiah is handed to him and, opening it, he finds the place where it is written.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: He rolls up the book, returns it to the attendant and sits, with all eyes fixed on him.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Today this scripture is fulfilled in your ears, on both sides.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: All bear witness and wonder at his gracious words and ask whether this is Joseph's son.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Jesus cites the proverb 'Physician, heal yourself' and the demand to do here what was done in Capharnaum.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Amen, no prophet is accepted in his own country; only English wording differs.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Many widows in Israel in Elijah's days when heaven was shut three years and six months with a great famine; 'terra' as earth or land is English wording.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Elijah was sent to none of them except a widow at Sarepta of Sidon.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Many lepers in Israel under Elisha, none cleansed except Naaman the Syrian.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: All in the synagogue are filled with anger on hearing this.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: They drive him out of the city to the brow of the hill to throw him down.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: He passes through their midst and goes his way.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: He goes down to Capharnaum in Galilee and teaches them on the Sabbaths.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: They are astonished at his teaching because his word was with authority ('in potestate').
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Latin says the man had 'an unclean demon' (daemonium immundum); the Greek says he had the spirit of an unclean demon.
cards.cause: A shorter expression in the Latin text, which lacks the word 'spirit'; its origin is unresolved.

cards.note: The demon's question and confession of the Holy One of God agree; Latin opens with 'Sine' (Let us alone) where the Greek has the exclamation Ah.
cards.cause: A lexical choice: the Latin renders the Greek interjection as an imperative of letting alone.

cards.note: Jesus rebukes the demon, orders silence and departure, and it throws the man down and leaves without harm.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Latin has 'fear' (pavor) coming on all where the Greek has amazement; the question about his word of authority and power agrees.
cards.cause: A lexical choice in the Latin rendering of the people's reaction.

cards.note: Word about him spreads to every place in the region.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Jesus leaves the synagogue for Simon's house, where Simon's mother-in-law has a high fever, and they ask him for her.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Latin says Jesus 'commanded' the fever (imperavit) where the Greek says he rebuked it; it leaves her and she serves them.
cards.cause: A lexical choice in the Latin rendering of the verb of rebuke.

cards.note: At sunset all bring their sick and he lays hands on each and heals them.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Demons cry out that he is the Son of God; he rebukes them and silences them because they knew he was the Christ.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: At daybreak he goes to a deserted place; the crowds find him and try to keep him from leaving.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: He must preach the kingdom of God to other cities too, for this he was sent.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Latin has him preaching in the synagogues 'of Galilee' (Galilaeae); the Greek has the synagogues of Judea.
cards.cause: A different textual reading; the Latin agrees with Greek manuscripts that read Galilee.

cards.note: Jesus stands by the lake of Gennesaret as people press to hear God's word; Latin has plural 'turbae' (crowds) where the Greek has a single crowd.
cards.cause: A difference of number in the Latin rendering.

cards.note: He sees two boats by the lake while the fishermen, having left them, wash their nets.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: He enters Simon's boat, asks him to put out a little, and teaches the crowds sitting in it.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: He tells Simon to put out into the deep and let down the nets for a catch.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Simon's reply about the fruitless night agrees; Latin has him let down 'the net' (rete, singular) where the Greek has the nets.
cards.cause: A difference of number; the Latin agrees with Greek manuscripts reading the singular.

cards.note: They enclose a great multitude of fish; Latin has 'their net' (rete eorum, singular) breaking where the Greek has their nets tearing.
cards.cause: A difference of number in the Latin text.

cards.note: Partners come and both boats are filled; Latin says they were 'almost sinking' (pene mergerentur) where the Greek says they began to sink.
cards.cause: A lexical choice in the Latin rendering of the Greek construction.

cards.note: Simon Peter falls at Jesus' knees asking him to depart, for he is a sinful man, Lord.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Amazement seizes him and all with him at the catch of fish.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: James and John, Simon's partners, are named on both sides; Latin says Simon will be 'catching men' (homines capiens) without the Greek sense of taking alive.
cards.cause: A lexical choice: the Latin uses a general verb of catching for the Greek verb of capturing alive.

cards.note: They bring the boats to land, leave everything and follow him.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: A man full of leprosy falls on his face and asks the Lord to cleanse him if he wills.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Jesus touches him, says 'I will; be cleansed', and the leprosy leaves at once.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: He orders silence and sends the man to the priest with the offering Moses commanded as a testimony.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: The report spreads all the more and great crowds gather to hear and be healed of their infirmities.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Jesus withdraws to pray; Latin has 'into the desert' (in desertum, singular) where the Greek has deserted places.
cards.cause: A difference of number in the Latin rendering.

cards.note: Pharisees and teachers from Galilee, Judea and Jerusalem are present on both sides; Latin says the Lord's power was there 'to heal them' (eos), the Greek for him to heal.
cards.cause: A different textual reading; the Latin agrees with Greek manuscripts that read 'them' instead of 'him'.

cards.note: Men carry a paralyzed man on a bed and seek to bring him in before Jesus.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Finding no way through the crowd, they lower him through the roof tiles on his bed before Jesus.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Seeing their faith, he says 'Man, your sins are forgiven you'.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: The scribes and Pharisees ask who this blasphemer is and who but God alone can forgive sins.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Jesus knows their thoughts and asks what they are thinking in their hearts.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Which is easier, to say 'Your sins are forgiven' or 'Rise and walk', on both sides.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: So they may know the Son of Man's authority to forgive, he tells the paralytic to rise, take his bed and go home.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: He rises at once, takes up his bed and goes home glorifying God.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: All are astonished, glorify God and, filled with fear, say they have seen wonders today.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Jesus sees the tax collector Levi at the tax booth and says 'Follow me'.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Leaving everything, he rises and follows him.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Levi holds a great feast in his house with many tax collectors and others at table.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: The Pharisees and their scribes grumble to his disciples about eating and drinking with tax collectors and sinners.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: The healthy do not need a physician, but the sick do.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: He came to call not the just but sinners to repentance.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: The contrast of fasting disciples and Jesus' eating disciples agrees; Latin frames it as a question with 'Quare' (why), the Greek as a statement.
cards.cause: A different textual reading; the Latin has the question, as some Greek manuscripts do.

cards.note: Latin speaks of the 'children of the bridegroom' (filios sponsi) where the Greek has sons of the wedding chamber; the point about fasting is the same.
cards.cause: A lexical choice in the Latin rendering of the Greek idiom for wedding guests.

cards.note: Days will come when the bridegroom is taken away, and then they will fast.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: The parable of the patch agrees; the Greek says one tears a patch from a new garment, while the Latin says only that no one puts a piece from a new garment on an old.
cards.cause: A difference of expression; the Latin follows a reading or rendering without the verb of tearing.

cards.note: New wine in old wineskins bursts them, spills and ruins the skins, on both sides.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Latin adds 'and both are preserved' (et utraque conservantur); the Greek says only that new wine must be put into fresh wineskins.
cards.cause: A different textual reading; the Latin has a clause found in some Greek manuscripts but not in the Greek text used here.

cards.note: Latin says the drinker of old wine does not 'immediately' (statim) want new and calls the old 'better' (melius); the Greek has no 'immediately' and calls it good.
cards.cause: A different textual reading; the Latin agrees with Greek manuscripts that have 'immediately' and the comparative.

cards.note: Latin dates the scene to the 'second first sabbath' (sabbato secundo, primo); the Greek says only 'on a Sabbath'. The plucking and rubbing of grain agree.
cards.cause: A different textual reading; the Latin has the term 'second-first', found in some Greek manuscripts but not in the Greek text used here.

cards.note: Some Pharisees ask why they do what is unlawful on the Sabbath; Latin adds that they said it 'to them' (illis).
cards.cause: A small addition in the Latin text, shared with some Greek manuscripts.

cards.note: Jesus asks whether they have not read what David did when he and his companions were hungry.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: David entered God's house, ate the bread of the presentation and gave it to his companions, though only priests may eat it.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Both declare the Son of Man Lord of the Sabbath; Latin adds 'also' (etiam).
cards.cause: A small addition in the Latin text, shared with some Greek manuscripts.

cards.note: On another Sabbath he teaches in the synagogue, where a man has a withered right hand.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: The scribes and Pharisees watch whether he will heal on the Sabbath to find grounds to accuse him.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Knowing their thoughts, he tells the man with the withered hand to rise and stand in the midst, and he does.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Jesus asks whether it is lawful on the Sabbath to do good or evil, to save life or destroy it.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: He looks around, commands the hand stretched out, and it is restored; Latin says he spoke 'to the man' (homini) where the Greek has 'to him'.
cards.cause: A noun for a pronoun in the Latin text.

cards.note: They are filled with folly or rage and discuss what to do to Jesus; 'insipientia' differs only in English wording.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: He goes to the mountain to pray and spends the night in prayer to God.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: At daybreak he calls his disciples and chooses twelve, whom he names apostles.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Simon called Peter, Andrew his brother, James, John, Philip and Bartholomew on both sides.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Matthew, Thomas, James of Alphaeus and Simon called Zelotes (the Zealot) agree.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Jude of James and Judas Iscariot the traitor appear on both sides; Latin 'Judam Jacobi' is the same bare genitive as the Greek.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: He stands on a level place with a crowd of disciples and a multitude from Judea, Jerusalem and the coast of Tyre and Sidon.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: They come to hear him and be healed, and those troubled by unclean spirits are cured.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: The whole crowd seeks to touch him, for power goes out from him and heals all.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Lifting his eyes to his disciples he blesses the poor, for theirs is the kingdom of God.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: The hungry now will be filled and those weeping now will laugh, on both sides.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Hatred, exclusion, reproach and rejection for the Son of Man agree; Latin has the future 'Beati eritis' (you shall be blessed) where the Greek has 'blessed are you'.
cards.cause: A difference of tense in the Latin rendering.

cards.note: Rejoicing, great reward in heaven and the fathers' treatment of the prophets agree; Latin 'exsultate' (exult) stands for the Greek 'leap'.
cards.cause: A lexical choice in the Latin rendering of the Greek verb for leaping.

cards.note: Woe to the rich; Latin says they 'have' (habetis) their consolation, while the Greek stresses that they have received it in full.
cards.cause: A lexical choice: the Latin uses a plain verb of having for the Greek verb of receiving in full.

cards.note: The woes on the filled and the laughing agree; Latin lacks 'now' with 'qui saturati estis' (you that are filled), where the Greek has 'filled now'.
cards.cause: A different textual reading; the Latin lacks 'now' in the first woe, as some Greek manuscripts do.

cards.note: Woe when people speak well of you, as their fathers did to the false prophets; Latin says 'homines' (men) without the Greek 'all'.
cards.cause: A different textual reading; the Latin lacks 'all', as some Greek manuscripts do.

cards.note: To those who hear: love your enemies and do good to those who hate you.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Bless those who curse you and pray for those who mistreat you; 'calumniantibus' differs only in English wording.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Offer the other cheek and do not withhold the tunic from one who takes the cloak.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Give to all who ask, and do not demand back what is taken.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Do to others as you wish them to do to you.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Loving those who love you earns no thanks or credit, since sinners do the same; 'gratia' is English wording.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Doing good to those who do good to you earns no credit; sinners do it too.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Lending in hope of return earns no credit; sinners lend to sinners to receive as much back.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Love enemies, do good, lend expecting nothing; great reward, sons of the Most High, for he is kind to the ungrateful and evil.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Be merciful as your Father is merciful; 'estote' and 'become' differ only in English wording.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Do not judge or condemn, and you will not be; forgive or release, and you will be forgiven.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Good measure, pressed down, shaken and overflowing is given into your lap; Latin speaks of 'the same measure' (eadem mensura) where the Greek has 'the measure you measure'.
cards.cause: A different textual reading; the Latin has 'same', as some Greek manuscripts do.

cards.note: Can the blind lead the blind? Will both not fall into a pit?
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Latin says everyone 'will be perfect, if he is like his master' (perfectus ... si sit sicut magister), the Greek that everyone fully trained will be like his teacher.
cards.cause: A different construction in the Latin rendering that reverses condition and result; its origin is unresolved.

cards.note: Why see the speck in your brother's eye and not notice the beam in your own?
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: The hypocrite must remove the beam from his own eye before taking the speck from his brother's.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: No good tree bears bad fruit and no bad tree good fruit.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Each tree is known by its fruit; no figs from thorns or grapes from a bramble.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: The good and evil person bring forth from the good and evil treasure, for the mouth speaks from the heart's abundance.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Why call me 'Lord, Lord' and not do what I say?
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Whoever comes, hears and does my words, I will show you whom he is like.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: The house on rock withstands the flood; Latin says it was 'founded on a rock' (fundata ... super petram), the Greek that it had been well built.
cards.cause: A different textual reading; the Latin agrees with Greek manuscripts giving the rock as the reason.

cards.note: The one who hears and does not act is like a house on the ground without foundation that falls in ruin when the river strikes.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Both say Jesus finished all his words in the people's hearing and entered Capernaum; the difference is English wording.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Both describe a centurion's servant who was sick, about to die, and precious to him; servant/slave is English wording.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Both have the centurion hear of Jesus and send Jewish elders asking him to come and save his servant; the difference is English wording.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Both have the elders plead earnestly that the centurion is worthy of this favour; the difference is English wording.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Both say he loves the nation and himself built the synagogue for them; the difference is English wording.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Both have Jesus near the house when the centurion sends friends saying he is unworthy for Jesus to enter his roof; the difference is English wording.

cards.note: Latin "pulmentarium" means something eaten with bread; the Saints renders the question as about fish. The answer No agrees.
cards.cause: A lexical nuance: the Latin word and the Saints English interpret the side dish differently.

cards.note: The command to cast on the right side and the net too full to draw agree; the difference is English wording.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Latin "tunica" (tunic) where the Saints has "outer garment"; the beloved disciple's word and Peter's leap agree.
cards.cause: A lexical choice in the garment term between the Latin and Greek.

cards.note: Latin "navigio" (boat) where the Saints has "little boat"; the two hundred cubits and the dragged net agree.
cards.cause: A lexical difference: the Greek uses a diminutive for the boat.

cards.note: On land they see a charcoal fire, fish laid on it, and bread, in both; the difference is English wording.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Jesus tells them to bring some of the fish just caught in both; the difference is English wording.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Peter draws the net with a hundred and fifty-three large fish, and it is not torn, in both; English wording only.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Latin "nemo audebat discumbentium" (none of those at table) where the Greek has none of the disciples; the invitation and question agree.
cards.cause: A different noun in the Latin reading for those present; its origin is unresolved.

cards.note: Jesus takes the bread and gives it, and the fish likewise, in both; the difference is English wording.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Latin "discipulis suis" (his disciples) where the Saints has "the disciples"; the third manifestation after the resurrection agrees.
cards.cause: A small pronoun present in the Latin reading and absent from the Greek text shown.

cards.note: The question about loving more than these, Peter's reply and "Feed my lambs" agree; Latin keeps diligis/amo distinct.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Latin repeats "Pasce agnos meos" (feed my lambs); the Greek has "Shepherd My sheep". The question and reply agree.
cards.cause: A different reading in the Latin tradition for the second commission; its origin is unresolved.

cards.note: Latin "Dixit ei" leaves the final speaker unnamed; the Greek names Jesus. The third question, Peter's grief and "Feed my sheep" agree.
cards.cause: A small difference in the speech introduction; the Greek reading names the speaker.

cards.note: Latin "ducet" (will lead) where the Greek says another will carry you; the girding and outstretched hands agree.
cards.cause: A lexical difference in the verb; its origin is unresolved.

cards.note: He signifies by what death Peter would glorify God and says "Follow me" in both; the difference is English wording.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Latin future "tradet" (shall betray) where the Greek has a present participle (is handing over); the beloved disciple at supper agrees.
cards.cause: A difference of tense between the Latin future and the Greek participle.

cards.note: Peter, seeing him, asks "Lord, and what about this man?" in both; the difference is English wording.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: This disciple testifies to these things and wrote them, and his testimony is true, in both; English wording only.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.

cards.note: Many other things Jesus did would fill more books than the world could hold, in both; English wording only.
cards.cause: The difference is one of English wording; the Latin and Greek agree here.
